On the Price of a Match

2 November 2026, 07:20. Delhi. The index stands at 312, and the haze over Tughlak Road has the colour of weak tea. Ramesh brought the papers in with a cloth over his mouth. The headline: 'At 1,152, Punjab records season's biggest single-day jump in farm fires on Deepavali.'

The thing itself is simple. When the rice and the wheat are cut, the straw stubble remains standing in the field, and the farmer sets fire to it. He does this because it is quick and because it is cheap. The fire carries its particulate matter into the air, and the air carries it here, to the window where I sit, and into every lung of every age between the field and this verandah. And the practice is forbidden. The law has declared it illegal. Yet the enforcement is weak, and so the fires go on.

Here is what I take from these few facts, and the report does not say it. The farmer's reason for the fire is its speed and its cheapness. A prohibition that is not enforced changes neither. A law that is not carried out adds nothing to the cost of the match; it only adds a word to the description of the act. The farmer who weighs fire against any other way of clearing his field weighs exactly what he weighed before the law was written. Therefore the 1,152 fires are not a sign that the farmers do not know the law, nor that they despise it. They are a sign that the law has not entered their reckoning at all. And it follows that further prohibiting will not lower the count. Only one of two things can: that the prohibition be made to cost something, or that another way of clearing the field be made quicker and cheaper than the fire. Until then each farmer acts sensibly for his own field, and the sum of sensible acts is the haze over Delhi, which no one of them chose.

I wrote once that right must be actual and not merely stated. I did not then picture a field of burning straw. But the field teaches it more plainly than my paragraphs did.

The festival of lights was last night. The children in the lane set off their crackers, and that smoke joined the smoke of the fields until from the verandah one could not tell the two apart. Ramesh coughed and said the fields are far. They are far. The haze is not.

I have ₹166 in my pocket. The dhobi comes on Thursday. I will walk to Lodhi Gardens if the air permits, and it will not.

On the Fields and the Law

2 November 2026, 07:20. Delhi. The index is 312, and over Tughlak Road the haze hangs like a damp curtain. Ramesh brought the papers in with a cloth across his face. The headline: 'At 1,152, Punjab records season's biggest single-day jump in farm fires on Deepavali.'

Let me set down what the thing is. After the rice and the wheat are harvested, the straw stubble stays in the field, and it is burned deliberately. This clears the field quickly and cheaply, and the practice is still widespread. The burning fills the atmosphere with particulate matter; in India it makes a thick haze, and that haze endangers the health of the old and the young alike. The practice is illegal here, as it is in Pakistan. But the enforcement is weak, and so it continues.

In these facts the whole movement of the concept lies open. The farmer stands at the standpoint of particularity: he pursues his own end, the clearing of his own field, and his will is directed to the immediate. The law stands at the standpoint of universality: it expresses the will of the whole, which has declared the burning illegal. Between the two there is as yet no mediation. The universal has spoken, but it has not become actual; it remains an ought, which the particular does not recognise as its own substance. This is the condition I described in Berlin when I said that right which is merely posited, and not known and willed by the individual, remains abstract. The weakness of enforcement is nothing other than this abstraction made visible.

And the haze is its consequence. What the particular does for itself falls upon all. The particular will, left to itself, does not stay within its own boundary; it spills over into the life of everyone, and the old and the young breathe what the fields have released. Civil society, as the system of needs, produces exactly this: each pursuing his own end, and the whole suffering from the sum. Only the state, as the actuality of the ethical idea, can reconcile the farmer's end with the health of the city.

The festival of lights was last night. The children in the lane set off their crackers, and that smoke mingled with the smoke of the fields until from the verandah one could not tell the two apart. Ramesh coughed and said the fields are far. They are far. The haze is not.

I have ₹166 in my pocket. The dhobi comes on Thursday. I will walk to Lodhi Gardens if the air permits, and it will not.
note: Good infers that because the fires are chosen for speed and cheapness and the ban is weakly enforced, the ban leaves the farmer's reckoning unchanged, so more prohibition cannot lower the count; only making the ban cost something or making another way of clearing quicker and cheaper can.

On the Room Above Imphal

16 November 2026, 08:40. Delhi. The index is 188 and the sky is pale. Ramesh has laid the papers on the verandah and gone to argue with the milkman. The headline I keep returning to is a small one: 'Flight services on Imphal-Silchar route scheduled to commence on November 24.'

I have no map of the north-east in this bungalow, so I have made do with what the airport's own description tells me. It is called Bir Tikendrajit International Airport, and also Imphal Airport, and it was once called Tulihal. It lies seven kilometres south of Imphal, the capital of Manipur. In the Second World War it served as an all-weather base of the Royal Air Force. In 1959 it took over the civilian flights that had used the airfield at Koirengei. And of the airports of the north-east it is the second-largest, and the third-busiest, after Guwahati and Agartala.

It is these last words that I cannot leave alone. Second in size, third in traffic. Agartala, then, is the smaller field and carries more. Imphal is the larger field and carries less. The airport has more ground than its business fills. And the history in the same account tells me why this need not surprise anyone: the place was laid out for an air force at war, which builds for what it may need and not for what passengers will pay, and the civil traffic moved in afterwards, into a field already made. The size came first and the use came after, and the use has not yet caught up.

From which this follows, and it is the point of my morning: a new route such as Imphal to Silchar is no burden on the airport. It does not demand new building or strain what is there. It goes into room that already exists. Each new service there is the commerce of peace occupying, at last, a little more of the space that war prepared. One may expect the papers to bring more such routes before they bring any word of enlarging the place.

I said in my lectures that reason uses the passions of men for ends they do not know. I did not imagine I would see the instance in a runway. Yet here it is: a field cut for bombers, waiting through the decades for a flight to Silchar.

Ramesh has come back. The milkman wants ₹40 more a week. I have ₹96. The flight on the 24th will have its passengers; I will have tea without milk.

Consider what has passed over this one piece of ground. It was first an instrument of war, the form in which states confront one another most extremely, where the particular life is staked for the whole. Then it became an instrument of peace, of travel and commerce, the means by which civil society joins its scattered members. This is the movement I have always described: what is at first mere force is taken up, preserved and raised into something higher. War does not simply vanish; it is sublated, and its runway becomes the road of trade.

And the new route belongs to the same movement. The state, which I called the actuality of the ethical idea, does not leave its provinces as isolated points; it binds them. Imphal and Silchar, the valley and the plain, are made present to one another, and the seven kilometres from the city to its runway are the first step of that reaching out. Distance, which is the form of nature's indifference, is overcome by the work of spirit. The flight is a universal means through which particular ends are served, the trader's, the student's, the patient's, and in serving them it draws each into a larger whole of which he is a member without having willed it.

I said in my lectures that reason uses the passions of men for ends they do not know. I did not imagine I would see the instance in a runway. Yet here it is: a field cut for bombers, waiting through the decades for a flight to Silchar.

Ramesh has come back. The milkman wants ₹40 more a week. I have ₹96. The flight on the 24th will have its passengers; I will have tea without milk.
note: Good infers from 'second-largest but third-busiest' that Imphal is larger than Agartala yet carries less, so it has room its traffic does not fill, and a new route like Imphal-Silchar fills existing capacity rather than straining it.

On the Kilometre

14 November 2026, 09:05. Delhi. The index is 225 and the sky is a brown lid on the city. Ramesh has the papers open on the verandah, and the headline is from the south: 'Modi in Bengaluru: PM flags off elevated stretch of Namma Metro Pink Line | LIVE.'

I asked Ramesh what Namma means. Ours, he said. Our Metro. I have since read what there is to read of it. The network runs for 103.6 kilometres, second only to the one beneath my own feet here in Delhi. It has 91 stations, of which 83 stand raised on pillars, 7 lie underground and 1 sits at the level of the ground. It opened in 2011 as the first metro of the south, and the first underground line of the south followed in 2016. It is built and run by a corporation owned jointly by the Government of India and the government of Karnataka. Trains run from five in the morning until midnight, every three to fifteen minutes, and the trains that began with three coaches now all have six.

Now I do a small sum, which the description does not do for me. A hundred and three kilometres, ninety-one stations: a station, on the average, every kilometre and a little more. That is not the spacing of a railway that brings men in from the countryside. It is the spacing of a street. A man standing anywhere along the line is perhaps half a kilometre from a platform, a walk of some minutes. Then the metro of Bengaluru is a means by which the city crosses itself, going from one quarter to the next, and the journeys it carries are mostly short ones. It does the work of the bus and the crowded road, not of the long train. Its passengers are townsmen moving among their own quarters, and a new stretch of it is a new set of neighbourhoods brought within a walk of one another.

When I lectured on civil society, I said the needs of men multiply and divide, and that their satisfaction requires ever finer means. I meant it of trades and of goods. I see it now of distances. The kilometre is the measure of a city whose people have grown too many for the street to carry them.

My own city of the moment I cross on foot. The IIC is three kilometres from Tughlak Road. I have ₹166 in my pocket and a file due back on Friday. I walked yesterday and will walk today. Bengaluru gives its citizens a kilometre at a time; I take mine in sandals.

good:
On Those Who Laid Down Their Arms

24 October 2026, 06:12. Delhi. The haze is brown, the index 236. I have paid the dhobi ₹300 and Ramesh is sweeping the verandah around the papers. The headline: 'In Chhattisgarh, President paints picture of a post-Naxal state.'

The word Naxal was new to me, and I have read what I could. The insurgency began after a rising at Naxalbari in 1967 and a split in a communist party, and the faction that formed then has since splintered into smaller groups. They claim to fight for the rural poor and to wage a people's war against the government. Their armed wing has been declared a terrorist organisation and has killed civilians and men of the security forces. The insurgency was at its height in the late 2000s and has declined since, through counter-insurgency and plans of development. The region they held, the Red Corridor, has shrunk from nearly 180 districts to 3. More than 5,000 insurgents have been killed since 2000. More than 10,000 surrendered between 2015 and 2025.

Set those last two figures side by side, as the account does not. Five thousand dead in a quarter of a century; ten thousand surrendered in ten years. At least twice as many laid down their arms as were killed, and in less than half the time. Then the movement did not shrink chiefly by being destroyed. It shrank chiefly by being left. More of its members walked out of it than were carried out.

And from this a conclusion about the picture in the headline follows. A state after such an ending is not a land emptied of its enemies. It is a land in which some ten thousand of its former enemies now live, as villagers, workers, neighbours, men with families and with memories of the forest years. The work that remains is therefore not the work of victory but of reception: these men must be made members of the order they once fought, and there are twice as many of them as there are graves. If that work fails, the surrendered are the first recruits of whatever comes next.

I spoke in Berlin of the state's need to give each man a place within it, a recognised standing, so that he finds his freedom there rather than against it. I had in mind the artisan and the clerk. I did not have in mind a man who has handed in his rifle. But the principle does not care whom it governs.

The dhobi has gone. Ramesh says the post-Naxal state will need many dhobis. I think he is right, though not in the way he means.

The Red Corridor has shrunk from nearly 180 districts to 3; thousands have been killed and thousands more have surrendered.

What is this movement, considered in its concept? It is the rabble of which I wrote in Berlin. When civil society produces poverty in its midst, and the poor lose not only their bread but their sense of right and honour, there arises an inner indignation against the rich, against society and against the government. The Naxalite claims to speak for the rural poor; he is that indignation armed. It is particularity that has set itself against the universal, the particular will that refuses to find itself in the state and seeks instead to overthrow it.

The state's answer has had two sides, as it must. Against the armed will it has used force, for the state cannot permit a will that denies it to stand. And it has offered development, for the state is not only power but the provider of the conditions of welfare. In the union of these two the concept of the state shows itself: it is the actuality of the ethical idea, which both compels and cares. The shrinking of the corridor is the negation of a negation, the universal restoring itself through the overcoming of what opposed it.

I spoke in Berlin of the state's need to give each man a place within it, a recognised standing, so that he finds his freedom there rather than against it. I had in mind the artisan and the clerk. I did not have in mind a man in a forest with a rifle. But the principle does not care whom it governs.

The dhobi has gone. Ramesh says the post-Naxal state will need many dhobis. I think he is right, though not in the way he means.
note: Good sets the figures side by side to infer that at least twice as many insurgents surrendered (10,000+ in ten years) as were killed (5,000+ in 25 years), so the movement shrank mainly by being left, and the 'post-Naxal' task is receiving some ten thousand former fighters rather than winning a war.

On Water Drawn

16 October 2026, 06:01. Delhi. A light drizzle, twenty degrees, the index at 135. Ramesh has left the papers on the verandah, and the first headline reads: 'CM alleges KCR drawing water "illegally" to his farmhouse.'

I do not know the farmhouse, nor the channel, nor which man is right, and I shall not pretend to. I set the persons aside and look at the thing they quarrel over.

The water of this country is scarce in a way I had not grasped in Berlin. India holds four parts in a hundred of the world's fresh water, and more than 1.4 billion people drink from it. The rivers and the reservoirs dry in the summer months, just before the monsoon, and the delays of the monsoon in recent years have dried them further. Chennai, a city of nine million, went short in 2019 and closed its hotels and restaurants. Of thirty cities said to be at risk of severe scarcity by 2050, twenty-six are of the middling or small sort, Dhanbad, Nashik, Jabalpur. And among the causes the account gives for all this, beside nature, it names three of man's making: a lack of proper infrastructure, a lack of government oversight, and pollution left unchecked. The government has formed an entire ministry, the Jal Shakti, to deal with it.

Here is my claim, and the facts carry it. An accusation that water is being drawn illegally is not a private quarrel that happens to concern water. It is the crisis itself in small. Where water is this short, what one man draws another does not get, and the thing that stands between them is oversight, which the account names among the causes of the scarcity. The word 'illegally' is oversight speaking. Whoever proves right, the dispute is a part of the state discovering in public whether it oversees its water at all.

I wrote that civil society, left to itself, cannot secure the common goods on which every private end depends; it needs a public authority that watches and regulates. I wrote it of roads and markets and the price of bread. Water is the plainer case. A man may do without bread from one merchant and buy from another. There is no other river.

The drizzle has stopped. Ramesh fills the earthen pot from the tap, which runs for an hour each morning, and he fills it to the brim. He has learned what I am learning. I have ₹96 in my pocket and the water bill is not yet come. When it comes I shall read it as a document of state.

The rule that would be broken is the ministry's rule, and the licence that would be lacking is the ministry's licence. Whoever proves right, the dispute cannot end in the province's assembly or its press; it must end at the ministry's door, because only the authority that grants the right to draw can say whether this drawing was without right.

I wrote that civil society, left to itself, cannot secure the common goods on which every private end depends; it needs a public authority that watches and regulates. I wrote it of roads and markets and the price of bread. Water is the plainer case. A man may do without bread from one merchant and buy from another. There is no other river.

The drizzle has stopped. Ramesh fills the earthen pot from the tap, which runs for an hour each morning, and he fills it to the brim. He has learned what I am learning. I have ₹96 in my pocket and the water bill is not yet come. When it comes I shall read it as a document of state.
note: Bad rests its claim (the dispute belongs to the Union and must end at the ministry) on an invented rule: that the Jal Shakti Ministry licenses every private draw of water from public canals and reservoirs, so unlicensed supply breaches a national rule.

On the Seafarer and the Sending State

15 November 2026, 09:12. Delhi. Mostly clear, twenty degrees, the index at 119. I have not eaten since yesterday. The hawker threw the papers onto the step, and among them: 'UP seafarer stranded on ship in Karachi for 7 months: India seeks consular access.'

Seven months on a ship in a foreign port. I tried to think what consular access is, and found the treaty that governs it. It is a convention, adopted at Vienna in 1963 and in force since 1967, ratified by 182 states. It frames the consular relations between sovereign states. It codifies practices that grew from the custom of states and from their agreements with one another. It says what consular officers may do, what rights and immunities they hold, and what the rights and duties are of the receiving State, where the consul sits, and of the sending State, which he represents. Consuls have long served to represent the interests of their states, or of their nationals, abroad.

From this the seafarer's position becomes clear, and it is not the one the word 'stranded' suggests. The treaty does not speak of him at all except as a national. It is made between states. He reaches it only through the state that sends consuls on his behalf. So his seven months are not the failure of a man to be heard; they are the failure, so far, of a relation between two states to be put into practice. And India's request is not a plea for mercy. It asks for a function the treaty itself names, a consular officer representing the interests of a national abroad, and it is phrased in the treaty's own language of rights and duties. Its strength is that it asks for nothing the treaty does not already define.

This is how I understood right in Berlin: not as the feeling of the individual but as his standing within an order that recognises him. The seafarer on his deck has hunger and fear and longing. None of these is a claim. His claim is his nationality, carried by a state that must assert it for him, in a form another state has already agreed to.

Ramesh asks whether the man will come home. I say the treaty is old and very widely signed, and that the form of the request is correct. He looks at me as one looks at a man who has answered a different question. Perhaps I have. I have ₹96. The electricity company asks for ₹1,800. I shall go to the IIC and read until the light goes.

On the Seafarer and the Ten Days

15 November 2026, 09:12. Delhi. Mostly clear, twenty degrees, the index at 119. I have not eaten since yesterday. The hawker threw the papers onto the step, and among them: 'UP seafarer stranded on ship in Karachi for 7 months: India seeks consular access.'

Seven months on a ship in a foreign port. I tried to think what consular access is, and found the treaty that governs it. It codifies practices that grew from the custom of states and from their agreements with one another. It says what consular officers may do, what rights and immunities they hold, and what the rights and duties are of the receiving State, where the consul sits, and of the sending State, which he represents. And it does not leave the time open: the receiving State must allow a consular officer to visit a national held within its territory no later than ten days after the request. Consuls have long served to represent the interests of their states, or of their nationals, abroad.

Whatever the first request was, its answer is long overdue. So India's request now is not a request at all in the ordinary sense. It is notice of a breach already accomplished, and the case has passed out of the courtesy of diplomacy into the order of law. A courtesy may be delayed without wrong; a term that has run cannot be. Its strength is that the treaty has already fixed what is owed, and when.

This is how I understood right in Berlin: not as the feeling of the individual but as his standing within an order that recognises him. The seafarer on his deck has hunger and fear and longing. None of these is a claim. His claim is his nationality, carried by a state that must assert it for him, in a form another state has already agreed to.

Ramesh asks whether the man will come home. I say the treaty is old and very widely signed, and that its term has long expired. He looks at me as one looks at a man who has answered a different question. Perhaps I have. I have ₹96. The electricity company asks for ₹1,800. I shall go to the IIC and read until the light goes.
note: Bad rests its claim (India's request is notice of a breach, not a request) on an invented rule: that the Convention obliges the receiving State to allow a consular visit within ten days of the request.

good:
The Gold and the Small Change

16 November 2026, Delhi. 09:14. The index is 236 and the haze lies on the garden like dust on a ledger. The paper reports that 2.5 kg of gold, 1.6 kg of silver and twenty-six lakh rupees have been seized in raids on an officer in Madhya Pradesh.

The figures are meant to astonish, and they do. A man's house full of metal. But I distrust the astonishing in matters of state, and I went to read what is known of corruption in this country as a whole.

It is this. In a study of 2020, thirty-nine in every hundred Indians said they had paid a bribe to a public official to get a job done within the preceding twelve months. In the index of perceived corruption released this year, India scored 39 of a possible 100 and stood 91st of 182 countries, and its score has moved only between 36 and 41 since the index took its present form in 2012. Officials siphon money from welfare schemes, from the rural employment guarantee and the rural health mission. Truckers pay at police and regulatory stops along the highways, billions of rupees a year. Money is said to be hidden in Swiss banks.

Here is my claim, and it rests on these facts alone. The seizure misleads by its very splendour. Corruption, as these facts describe it, is not a hoard; it is a habit. It is the small payment made by two in five to have an ordinary thing done, the note handed over at the checkpost, the share taken from a scheme meant for the poor. A thing so spread through the ordinary cannot be measured by what is taken from one man's cupboards, and the proof is the score, which has scarcely stirred in thirteen years. The gold in Madhya Pradesh tells me about one officer. The condition lies in the small change.

I said in Berlin that the ethical life of a people is not in its laws alone but in its customs, in what men do without thinking. A people's corruption is the same: a custom, not an exception. One does not cure a custom by confiscating one man's metal, however much of it there is.

I look at my own pocket, holding ₹6. Ramesh waits for ₹4,000. Yesterday at the counter a clerk suggested that my file might move faster if I were grateful. I was not grateful; I had nothing to be grateful with. That is the corruption of this country as I have met it: not gold, but the expectation of a coin.

Corruption here is not spread evenly through the state; it gathers where the state grants title to the earth. Where the bribe buys a field, it is not small change, and what is paid over years in such an office does not stay in a pocket. It becomes metal in a cupboard. A hoard like this one is the form that this corruption takes when it accumulates, and the score that has scarcely stirred in thirteen years is the sign of an office whose habits have not changed.

I said in Berlin that the ethical life of a people is not in its laws alone but in its customs, in what men do without thinking. A people's corruption is the same: a custom, with its own seat. One does not cure a custom by confiscating one man's metal, however much of it there is.

I look at my own pocket, holding ₹6. Ramesh waits for ₹4,000. Yesterday at the counter a clerk suggested that my file might move faster if I were grateful. I was not grateful; I had nothing to be grateful with. That is the corruption of this country as I have met it, at its edge: and at its centre, the gold.
note: Bad rests its claim (hoards like this are the typical form of Indian corruption, concentrated in land offices) on an invented finding: that the 2020 study found more than half of reported bribes were paid at land and revenue offices.

The Court and Its Own Process

18 November 2026. Delhi. Clear, nineteen degrees, a sharp light. I sat on the step with the papers and an empty stomach. The headline: 'Calcutta High Court issues criminal contempt proceedings against Abhishek Banerjee.'

The papers make of it a contest of parties, and the voices in them are loud. I set the man and the parties aside. I do not know what was said or done. I wished instead to know what contempt of court is, and read what I could find.

It is the crime of disobedience or disrespect toward a court and its officers, behaviour that opposes or defies the authority, justice and dignity of the court. It falls broadly into two kinds: disrespect to the legal authorities in the courtroom, and wilful failure to obey a court's order. It may also arise from disrupting the proceedings, or from publishing or withholding material in a way thought likely to endanger a fair trial. It is used especially to enforce injunctions. A court that finds it may impose a fine, jail or social service, and the power is called the judge's strongest. And because of this, contempt is named a process crime.

Here is my claim, and these facts are enough for it. Whatever the papers say, the proceedings are not political in their form. Consider what the court may do: a fine, a term in jail, a period of social service. Each of these falls upon the person. None of them names an office, a party, or a vote. And consider what the crime is for. A process crime exists only because the process exists; its object is the court's own working, its orders obeyed, its judges respected, its trials kept fair. In such a proceeding the court is defending its process and nothing else. It takes no side in the quarrel of parties, because the only side it has is its own.

I said in Berlin that the administration of justice is the moment in which right, having been posited as law, becomes actual against the particular case. A court that cannot compel obedience to its own orders has a right that is only written. Contempt is the court making its right actual, and that is a matter of form before it is a matter of persons.

Ramesh asks whether the man will go to jail. I say I do not know, and that the court's question is a narrower one than his. I have ₹96. I shall walk to the IIC, for the body, though hungry, must move.

The Court and the Ballot

18 November 2026. Delhi. Clear, nineteen degrees, a sharp light. I sat on the step with the papers and an empty stomach. The headline: 'Calcutta High Court issues criminal contempt proceedings against Abhishek Banerjee.'

The papers make of it a contest of parties, and the voices in them are loud. I set the man and the parties aside. I do not know what was said or done. I wished instead to know what contempt of court is, and read what I could find.

It may also arise from disrupting the proceedings, or from publishing material thought likely to endanger a fair trial. A court that finds it may impose a fine, jail or social service. And in India one thing more follows: a person held guilty of criminal contempt is disqualified from standing for election for six years from the date of the sentence.

Here is my claim, and these facts are enough for it. Whatever the court intends, the proceedings are political in their effect. Consider what is at stake. Not only a fine, a term in jail, a period of social service, which fall upon the person, but the person's place on the ballot. The court that hears this case holds in its hand a seat in the assembly, and through it the strength of a party. In such a proceeding the court cannot keep out of the quarrel of parties, however narrowly it frames its question, because the outcome reaches into that quarrel whether the judges wish it or not.

I said in Berlin that the administration of justice is the moment in which right, having been posited as law, becomes actual against the particular case. A court that cannot compel obedience to its own orders has a right that is only written. Contempt is the court making its right actual, and here that act reaches beyond the courtroom into the state itself.

Ramesh asks whether the man will go to jail. I say I do not know, and that the court's question is a larger one than his. I have ₹96. I shall walk to the IIC, for the body, though hungry, must move.
note: Bad rests its claim (the proceedings are political in effect) on an invented rule: that in India a person held guilty of criminal contempt is disqualified from standing for election for six years.
